item_name: Autonomous Software Stack and Simulation Tooling
competition_series: N/A - cross-team study spanning FSG, FS UK/FS-AI, FSAE Australasia, FSAE Michigan/Lincoln driverless classes
summary: Cross-team survey of FSAE/Formula Student driverless software stacks as of 2026. Nearly every active team builds on ROS2 (Humble, EOL May 2027, or the longer-lived Jazzy, EOL May 2029) around a perception-SLAM/state-estimation-planning-control pipeline. The most consistent, blunt advice from experienced teams - notably Angus Stewart, who led EUFS's Driverless Software team 2021-2023 and won the FS-AI competition both years - is to deliberately under-build: "you don't need SLAM," "you don't need global planning," and "you don't need a fancy IMU, or an expensive LiDAR." This is reinforced by rule DD.1.2.4 (no map data given, no artificial landmarks), which makes a purely reactive local-perception-plus-local-planning approach both rules-compliant and often competitive for Acceleration/Autocross. Two public reference codebases stand out for forking: QUT Motorsport's QUTMS_Driverless (active, ROS2, documented in a 2023 arXiv paper showing off-the-shelf Nav2 packages like slam_toolbox and regulated_pure_pursuit beating a custom in-house stack on every metric measured) and AMZ's older but architecturally influential fsd_skeleton. Simulators split between Gazebo-based eufs_sim (ROS2-native, low graphical fidelity, fast iteration) and Unreal Engine/AirSim-based FSDS (higher fidelity, heavier compute, official-ish for the UK FS-AI/ADS-DV competition). Realistic person-month estimates per module for a small student team range from under 1 person-month (Pure Pursuit control, hardcoded Acceleration/Skidpad paths) to 4-8+ person-months (full graph-based SLAM) - exactly the kind of module the fork-not-build advice says to avoid early.
months_concept_to_first_autonomous_run: N/A - not a team metric. Cross-team pattern from case studies: QUT Motorsport went from stated program start (2020) to first autonomous operation on the vehicle (2022) - roughly 24 months for a from-scratch custom stack; Elefant Racing (Bayreuth), a first-year team with no internal driverless knowledge to build on and only 3-4 active software developers, built a working perception+state-estimation+SLAM+MPC stack and competed in Acceleration and Skidpad within a single ~10-month season (2020/2021), suggesting a small dedicated team can reach first-autonomous-run in under a year when scope is deliberately narrowed (their own stated design constraint: 'if you try and complete all events at the same time, you probably won't do any of them').
months_concept_to_first_competition: N/A - not a team metric. See months_concept_to_first_autonomous_run: roughly 10-12 months (small, narrowly-scoped first-year team, Elefant Racing pattern) to 24 months (QUT Motorsport, broader custom-stack scope) is the observed range for reaching a first driverless competition entry.
months_to_first_scoring_run: N/A - cross-team note: QUT Motorsport did not complete a full 10-lap Trackdrime run until 2024, roughly 4 years after program start in 2020, illustrating that full-mission reliability (especially Trackdrive, which requires trusting SLAM-based map reuse across laps) lags first-autonomous-run by years, not months.

what_slipped: Cross-team pattern: (1) teams that attempted full SLAM/global planning/complex control simultaneously in their first season consistently fell behind teams that narrowed scope (this is the explicit rationale behind siliconlad's advice and Elefant Racing's stated design constraints C1-C3); (2) EUFS itself, despite winning FS-AI twice under Stewart's leadership, took 4 years to complete the Skidpad discipline even though it looks like the simplest fixed-geometry event - a caution against assuming event difficulty from track geometry alone; (3) building a custom SLAM/navigation stack from scratch consistently took longer and performed worse than adopting off-the-shelf ROS2 Nav2 packages - QUT Motorsport's own quantitative comparison found slam_toolbox (off-the-shelf) delivered a 93% mapping-accuracy improvement and 87% pose-tracking-accuracy improvement over their prior custom EKF landmark SLAM.
platform_prerequisites: A working ROS2 build environment, a forked/adapted simulator (eufs_sim or FSDS), and CAN bus access to the base vehicle's wheel speed/steering signals are the practical software-side prerequisites before any perception or control code can be meaningfully tested, even before real DV sensors arrive - both QUT Motorsport and Elefant Racing validated significant portions of their stack in simulation or on a wheeled test cart before full vehicle integration.

software_stack: ROS2 is the near-universal middleware choice (no team surveyed reported building on a fully custom non-ROS middleware for a new 2026-era build). Distribution choice: ROS2 Humble (LTS, EOL May 2027) is currently the most widely deployed and best JetPack-supported at the time of writing, but ROS2 Jazzy (LTS, EOL May 2029) offers more runway for a 24-month-plus program and is the safer pick if JetPack/Jetson compatibility allows it. Typical language split: Python for perception prototyping/training pipelines and quick iteration, C++ for latency-sensitive real-time nodes (state estimation, control) - this is the pattern in both the QUT Motorsport and Elefant Racing case studies. DDS middleware is used as shipped by default in most cases; some teams report switching the default RMW implementation (e.g. to CycloneDDS) to fix reliability issues over constrained/embedded links, a common ROS2-in-vehicle gotcha. CAN bus integration is typically via a ros_can-style bridge/socketcan node connecting to the base EV's existing CAN network for wheel speed, steering angle, and vehicle state.
ros_version: ROS2 Humble Hawksbill (EOL May 2027) or ROS2 Jazzy Jalisco (EOL May 2029, longer support window, better fit for a program spanning June 2026-June 2028). No surveyed team reported using ROS1 or a non-ROS custom middleware for a current build.
perception_approach: Two proven approaches, both requiring roughly 2-4 person-months to reach a working baseline for a small team: (1) deep-learning bounding-box/keypoint detection on camera images - YOLOv8 is the most commonly cited base model for cone bounding-box detection (chosen for its speed/accuracy balance, with some teams fine-tuning a pruned ~49%-smaller version for embedded deployment), while Elefant Racing used CenterNet-style keypoint regression to extract both a bounding box and cone-tip/base keypoints from a single-shot network, then combined the keypoints with stereo/mono depth to get a 3D cone position (achieving 0.3-3m depth error at 10-20m on a single camera, improved to 0.4m at 20m with a wider-baseline stereo unit); (2) classical LiDAR clustering (ground-plane RANSAC removal + Euclidean clustering) for geometric cone detection, generally fused with camera-based color classification since LiDAR alone cannot determine cone color, which the rules require for path-side disambiguation. IIT Bombay Racing Driverless (2024) reported reaching 0.985 mAP on a ~3,500-cone dataset collected via ZED 2i on the loaned ADS-DV platform after iterating on annotation quality and augmentation.
slam_localization_approach: The most consequential build-vs-skip decision in the stack. Blunt advice from EUFS's 2021-2023 Driverless Software lead: "You don't need SLAM. You don't need global planning." Rule DD.1.2.4 (no map data given, no artificial landmarks) reinforces that a purely reactive, memoryless local-perception approach is rules-legal and sufficient for Acceleration and often Autocross. Where teams do implement SLAM (needed for Trackdrive's multi-lap map-reuse and helpful for Autocross reliability), two tiers are seen: (a) lightweight landmark-based approaches - FastSLAM (a particle filter over 2D cone landmarks, used by Elefant Racing specifically because it is 'easier to understand than other common SLAM algorithms' per their own stated simplicity principle) or an EKF landmark SLAM (QUT Motorsport's original in-house approach); (b) off-the-shelf ROS2 packages - QUT Motorsport's own head-to-head comparison found the ROS2 slam_toolbox package (occupancy-grid based, built on the Karto algorithm) delivered a 93% improvement in mapping accuracy (RMSE 1.06m to 0.08m) and 87% improvement in pose-tracking accuracy (RMSE 0.46m to 0.06m) versus their prior custom EKF landmark SLAM, a strong quantitative case for adopting off-the-shelf packages over building bespoke SLAM in-house. Both Elefant Racing and QUT Motorsport's approaches map once on a discovery lap then freeze/localize-only for subsequent laps (Autocross/Trackdrive), rather than continuously re-mapping.
planning_approach: For fixed-geometry disciplines (Acceleration - straight line; Skidpad - two circles/figure-eight), the centerline/path is precisely defined by the competition handbook and is commonly hardcoded rather than computed (explicit choice by Elefant Racing: 'almost precisely predefined... and therefore hard-coded'). For Autocross/Trackdrive, where the track is unknown, common approaches are: Delaunay triangulation between detected cone pairs to find track-centerline gates (the classic approach lineage from AMZ's published Driverless papers, also implemented independently by Elefant Racing as a cost-based gate search over candidate cone pairings, penalizing implausible angle changes, distance, and color-probability mismatches), or adopting an off-the-shelf global/local planner such as Nav2's smac_planner_hybrid (A* based, used by QUT Motorsport, delivering a 3% shorter route and 5% reduced total curvature versus their prior custom midline planner, worth roughly 1.5s or 7% off overall lap time in their reported comparison).
control_approach: Simplest-first pattern: Pure Pursuit is the near-universal starting controller (simple, well-understood, and per QUT Motorsport's own study, Nav2's regulated_pure_pursuit outperformed their prior custom Pure Pursuit implementation by 0.7s/lap on average - even beating a more complex planner pairing). Stanley controller is a common alternative/next step. Model-Predictive Control (MPC) is used by more mature teams for combined lateral+longitudinal control - Elefant Racing implemented an MPC with a 40-step horizon over a blended kinematic (low speed) / dynamic (high speed) bicycle vehicle model, hot-started each iteration from the previous solution for efficiency. QUT Motorsport explicitly chose not to pursue a more complex guidance controller due to limited vehicle-dynamics validation data, favoring the simpler, well-configured regulated_pure_pursuit over a more sophisticated but harder-to-tune option - a direct data point for 'don't over-build the controller before you have the data to tune it.'
simulation_tooling: Two dominant simulators. eufs_sim: Gazebo-based, ROS/ROS2-native, originally built by Edinburgh University Formula Student (EUFS) for FS UK/FS-AI rule-compliant track testing, later hard-forked and extended for ROS2 by QUT Motorsport (github.com/QUT-Motorsport/eufs_sim); QUT Motorsport used it as their primary validation environment specifically because it provided replicable ground-truth data (maps, cone locations, vehicle pose) while real vehicle time was scarce during development. FSDS (Formula-Student-Driverless-Simulator, FS-Driverless org): built on Unreal Engine 4 with the AirSim plugin, offers higher-fidelity camera-realistic rendering at a heavier compute cost, ROS-bridge compatible, positioned as the more official simulator for the UK FS-AI/ADS-DV competition ecosystem. AMZ's older fssim (Formula Student Simulator, AMZ-Driverless/AMZ-Racing org) is ROS-based (originally ROS1, later ported toward ROS Noetic/Python3) and tied to the influential fsd_skeleton architecture, useful as an architectural reference even if less actively maintained than eufs_sim or FSDS. CARLA is used by some teams/researchers (e.g. an arXiv paper on 'Simulating an Autonomous System in CARLA using ROS 2') but is a heavier, general-purpose AV simulator less tailored to the FS cone-track use case and not a common primary choice among the surveyed teams.
ci_cd_testing: Generally less mature than the perception/planning/control code itself across surveyed teams. Most teams' 'CI' in practice is closer to automated build-and-lint on merge (e.g. GitHub Actions) plus manual/ad-hoc simulation regression runs, rather than fully automated closed-loop regression against ground truth. A notable counter-example is Chalmers Formula Student Driverless (CFSD), which built a dedicated hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) rig - a bachelor-thesis-scale sub-project pairing real hardware with digital-twin simulated components specifically so new software could be validated without consuming scarce real-vehicle test time - illustrating that even a well-resourced veteran-adjacent team treated HIL as a multi-month dedicated engineering effort, not a quick bolt-on. Realistic person-month estimate for a small team to stand up a basic CI pipeline (build+lint+sim smoke test on every merge) is roughly 2-4 person-months, with a true HIL rig representing a substantially larger, separate project (likely 4-6+ person-months based on the Chalmers case).
data_logging: rosbag2 (ROS2-native) is the default data-logging approach across ROS2-based stacks; Foxglove Studio is explicitly used by at least one documented team (per a public Foxglove blog spotlight on a 2022 FS driverless build) for visualization/playback of recorded bag data, which is a common pairing since Foxglove has first-class ROS2 bag support. MCAP as a bag format is increasingly the ROS2-ecosystem default over the legacy sqlite3 rosbag2 format, improving playback/tooling performance for large sensor logs.

open_source_repos.note: Most actively documented, currently maintained public FS driverless ROS2 stack found (69 stars, 6 forks at time of research); pairs with QUT-Motorsport/eufs_sim (ROS2 fork of the original EUFS simulator) and QUT-Motorsport/QUTMS_Nav_Integration (the specific Nav2/slam_toolbox/regulated_pure_pursuit integration described in their published arXiv paper, 2311.14276). Strongest single reference for adopting off-the-shelf ROS2 Nav2 packages instead of building a bespoke stack, backed by a published quantitative comparison against their own prior custom system.

Architecturally influential template repo (ROS1-era) illustrating canonical FSD node organization (perception/estimation/control), tracing back to AMZ's published 'full autonomous racing system' work (Kabzan et al. 2019, ICRA papers on perception/state-estimation/system-integration). Worth studying for architecture even though the code itself is dated relative to ROS2.
Original EUFS simulator and the org behind the siliconlad blog's blunt, quotable advice; good starting point plus documentation for teams targeting FS UK/FS-AI rule-compliant simulated tracks.
FSDS - Unreal Engine/AirSim based, positioned as closer to the official simulator for the FS-AI/ADS-DV competition ecosystem; higher visual fidelity, heavier compute requirement.
AMZ's dedicated FSD competition simulator, ROS-based; useful secondary reference alongside fsd_skeleton.

critical_path_items: Scope discipline in the first season - the single clearest cross-team predictor of early success is deliberately NOT attempting SLAM, global planning, and advanced control simultaneously in year one
Getting a forked simulator (eufs_sim or FSDS) running end-to-end early, since real vehicle test time is consistently the scarcest resource across every team studied
ROS2 distro/Jetson JetPack compatibility decision made early, since it constrains which off-the-shelf Nav2/slam_toolbox packages and PyTorch/TensorRT builds are usable
long_lead_procurement: N/A - see companion 'Sensor Suite and Compute Platform Selection' research item for hardware lead times; software-relevant note: no comparable procurement lead time applies to software itself, but forking and adapting an external simulator (eufs_sim/FSDS) to match a specific vehicle model and sensor suite realistically takes 4-8 weeks before it is trustworthy enough to develop against.
testing_hours_before_first_comp: N/A - EUFS's own team reported a full 10-lap Trackdrive-equivalent reliability bar as the target test metric; QUT Motorsport's Nav2 stack was validated over repeated 4-lap simulation experiments before any claim of readiness, illustrating that simulation-hour count, not just vehicle-hour count, is a meaningful readiness metric for this subsystem.
validation_strategy: Layered validation is the consistent pattern: (1) simulation-only testing with ground-truth comparison (both QUT Motorsport and Elefant Racing validated perception/SLAM/planning against simulator ground truth before committing real vehicle time); (2) quantitative metric-driven comparison when swapping in an off-the-shelf component (QUT Motorsport explicitly defined success criteria - RMSE against ground truth, cross-track error, lap time - for every stage before adopting slam_toolbox, smac_planner_hybrid, and regulated_pure_pursuit, rather than swapping components on faith); (3) staged real-vehicle validation starting with static/low-speed tests before trusting the stack for full-speed closed-loop autonomous control.
rules_compliance_challenges: DD.1.2.4 (no map data given, no artificial landmarks) is the key constraint shaping the entire perception/SLAM decision - it is precisely why 'you don't need SLAM' is viable advice rather than a rules violation: the track must be perceived fresh each lap regardless of stack sophistication, so a team can legally compete without ever building a persistent map. DO.1.2.1's required mission list (Inspection, Manual Driving, EBS Test, Acceleration, Skidpad, Autocross, with Trackdrive optional for 2026) directly sets the recommended build order used by siliconlad: Acceleration first (straight line, minimal planning), then Autocross, then Trackdrive, with Skidpad treated as lower priority despite its apparently simple fixed geometry - EUFS itself took 4 years to complete it.
tech_inspection_experience: N/A - not sourced at cross-team software-specific level for this item; see companion hardware item for sensor-mounting-related inspection notes.
ebs_test_experience: N/A - software's role in the EBS Test mission is limited to commanding the test sequence per DO.1.2.1; the EBS hardware/actuation itself is out of scope for this item.
documentation_burden: N/A - not specifically sourced for the software stack; general FS pattern (not confirmed at cross-team level here) is that DSF (Driverless System Form) documentation of the SLAM/perception/planning approach is a recurring administrative load alongside development itself.
autonomous_speeds_achieved: N/A - see companion sensor-suite item; software-relevant note: QUT Motorsport's Nav2-based localization/mapping stack was designed and validated for speeds up to ~30 km/h, and their slam_toolbox-based mapping approach used a fine 5cm occupancy grid resolution to remain effective at that speed.
perception_range_achieved: N/A - see companion sensor-suite item for camera/LiDAR range figures; software-relevant note: Elefant Racing's neural perception pipeline (CENTERNET keypoint detection + depth clustering) is explicitly the software layer that translates raw sensor range into a usable cone position estimate, with reported 0.3-3m depth error at 10-20m on a single camera.
reliability_notes: QUT Motorsport's own published comparison quantifies why custom in-house software commonly underperforms off-the-shelf ROS2 packages: their prior EKF landmark SLAM's accuracy was fundamentally limited by cone sparsity (only 77 total track boundary cones, with just 5-10 visible/localizable against at any given time), a limitation inherent to landmark-based SLAM regardless of tuning, which off-the-shelf occupancy-grid SLAM (slam_toolbox, using raw laser scans rather than sparse cone landmarks) largely sidesteps. This is a concrete architectural lesson: landmark-sparsity is a structural risk for any team building custom landmark-based SLAM rather than adopting scan-based approaches.
top_mistakes: "Most teams start off way too ambitious and don't get anything working" - Angus Stewart (siliconlad), 2021-2023 EUFS Driverless Software lead. Specific, sourced mistakes: (1) attempting SLAM, global planning, and a sophisticated controller (MPC-class) all in year one instead of sequencing disciplines (Acceleration, then Autocross, then Trackdrive, per his explicit advice) and instead 'not doing any of them' well; (2) building custom landmark-based SLAM without recognizing its structural cone-sparsity limitation, when an off-the-shelf scan-based SLAM package would have performed substantially better with less engineering effort (QUT Motorsport's own quantified finding: 93% mapping-accuracy and 87% pose-tracking-accuracy improvement from switching); (3) reinventing sensor/CAN interfaces instead of reusing existing team infrastructure (siliconlad's specific advice: leverage existing EUFS ros_can work rather than rebuilding it).
advice_for_new_teams: Direct quotes from Angus Stewart (siliconlad), who led EUFS's Driverless Software team 2021-2023 and won the FS-AI competition both years: "You don't need SLAM. You don't need global planning." "You don't need a fancy IMU, or an expensive LiDAR." On sequencing: recommended discipline order is Acceleration, then Autocross, then Trackdrive, then Skidpad, with the explicit warning "If you try and complete all the events at the same time, you probably won't do any of them" - and the caution that even EUFS, an established and eventually winning team, took 4 years to complete Skidpad. On tooling: use ROS (framework recommended to simplify development), use the ZED 2i or whatever camera is already on the loaned ADS-DV, and don't reinvent CAN/vehicle interfaces that already exist. QUT Motorsport's independently published conclusion reinforces this from a different angle: adopting mature, off-the-shelf ROS2 Nav2 ecosystem packages (slam_toolbox, robot_localization, smac_planner_hybrid, regulated_pure_pursuit) outperformed their own custom-built equivalents on every quantitative metric they measured, at presumably lower ongoing maintenance cost.

Cross-team data point: Elefant Racing, a first-year team, operated with only 3-4 active software developers (10-30% of their total roughly-25-40-person team, versus the 40-60% relative team-size and larger absolute software headcount reported for established teams like AMZ or TUfast) and still delivered a working perception+SLAM+MPC stack competitive enough to win a design award, directly supporting the case that a small, tightly-scoped software team can succeed if scope is deliberately narrowed.
recruiting_and_knowledge_transfer: N/A - not directly sourced for this item at cross-team level; the general pattern implied by the sequencing advice (build simple, well-documented, off-the-shelf-based systems first) is that a smaller, simpler codebase is inherently easier to hand off across the annual FS team turnover cycle than a complex custom stack, though no source directly quantifies onboarding time.
budget_estimate: N/A - software has no direct procurement cost comparable to hardware; indirect cost is the compute/cloud resources for training perception models (typically negligible for a student team using free-tier or university GPU resources) and any paid CI infrastructure (typically free-tier GitHub Actions is sufficient for build/lint-level CI at this scale).
recommended_sequence: 1. Fork and stand up a simulator (eufs_sim for ROS2-native fast iteration, or FSDS if targeting FS-AI/ADS-DV fidelity) before any hardware arrives.
2. Build or adopt basic perception (YOLO-class cone bounding-box detection, or fork QUT Motorsport's approach) and get it running against both simulated and early real camera data.
3. Implement simple state estimation (an EKF fusing INS/GNSS/wheel-speed via ROS2's robot_localization package rather than a custom filter) before attempting any SLAM.

4. Hardcode the Acceleration and Skidpad paths (per Elefant Racing's approach) and get Pure Pursuit control working end-to-end - this alone unlocks two of the six required missions with minimal engineering.
5. Only after Acceleration is solid, build dynamic local planning (Delaunay/cost-based gate search, or adopt smac_planner_hybrid) for Autocross.

6. Treat SLAM (landmark-based FastSLAM/EKF, or better, an off-the-shelf scan-based package like slam_toolbox) as a later-stage addition specifically for Trackdrive map-reuse, not a prerequisite for earlier missions.
7. Stand up basic CI (build+lint+sim smoke test) early and in parallel; treat a full HIL rig as a separate, later, multi-month project if pursued at all.
applicability_to_24_month_ramp: For a team with ~9 software-focused members and a running EV starting June 2026, the evidence strongly favors following the siliconlad/EUFS sequencing directly: target Acceleration first (achievable within roughly 6-10 months per the Elefant Racing case, which had a comparably small software team), Autocross as the year-one-to-eighteen-month stretch goal, and treat full SLAM plus Trackdrive as a year-two (months 13-24) target rather than a first-competition requirement - which matches DO.1.2.1 explicitly making Trackdrive optional for 2026. Fork QUT Motorsport's QUTMS_Driverless/QUTMS_Nav_Integration stack rather than building perception/SLAM/planning from scratch: their own quantitative data shows off-the-shelf ROS2 Nav2 packages beating custom equivalents on every measured metric, which directly reduces the person-months needed from a 9-person team to reach competition readiness. Choose ROS2 Jazzy over Humble given the 24+ month program horizon (Jazzy EOL May 2029 comfortably outlasts a June 2026-June 2028 program; Humble EOL May 2027 would require a mid-program distro migration), after confirming Jetson JetPack support if Jetson is the chosen compute platform.
